html:
The Ópata were an Indigenous people of the river valleys of northern and central Sonora, Mexico. They had three main divisions, the Tegüima, the Eudeve and the Jova, and spoke Uto-Aztecan languages.

They lived in farming towns along the Sonora, Moctezuma and Bavispe rivers, growing maize, beans, squash and cotton with irrigation. In 1540 the expedition of Francisco Vázquez de Coronado passed through their valleys on its way north. Jesuit missions from New Spain came in the 1600s.

The Ópata became allies of the Spanish and fought with them against the Apache. Over time they married into the mestizo population of Sonora, and their languages died out in the 1900s. Neighbours included the Pima, the Yaqui and the Rarámuri.
